The band had gone quiet and the jeep was packed with the bride's suitcases when Vaibhav noticed Yamini by the mango tree, wiping her cheeks with her dupatta and grinning at the same time. She had been fussing over her little sister's veil all morning. He nearly rushed over to ask who had upset her, then saw the grin was real. He walked up and said, "Can I stand here with you?" She nodded.
"She looked so happy," Yamini said, laughing and sniffing together. "And the house will be so quiet now. And I'm glad it's done, I was tired of worrying about the caterers."
Vaibhav passed her his handkerchief. "I'm feeling it too, honestly. Come, let's wave until the jeep turns the corner."
They did, both a bit wet-eyed.

qa.q: Where was Yamini standing when Vaibhav noticed her?
qa.a: Yamini was standing by the mango tree.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Yamini describe?
qa.a: Happiness that her sister looked so happy, sadness that the house will be quiet, and relief that the wedding worry is over. Her tears and grin at once fit that mix, though Vaibhav could only know by asking.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do that helped in the moment?
qa.a: He asked to stand beside her, listened, offered his handkerchief and shared that he felt it too. He did not assume she was upset.

qa.q: What might have happened if Vaibhav had rushed in asking who upset her?
qa.a: Yamini might have felt misunderstood and had to explain herself, and the shared moment could have turned into defending her happiness.

grounding: Illustrates crying and smiling at once at a wedding, joy, relief and loss together, with a listener who simply asks and shares the moment.

Ines saw her friend before Olga saw her: Olga, on tiptoe at the arrivals barrier, holding a paper sign that said "Welcome home, idiot." Then Olga spotted her, and her face did two things at once. Her mouth stretched into a huge smile and tears ran straight down. Ines stopped with her suitcase, unsure. Was something wrong? She waited.
"Say something," Olga said, laughing, wiping her eyes. "I'm not sad. Okay, a little sad. Three years."
Ines dropped the bag and hugged her. "I was going to ask. I couldn't tell which one it was."
"Both," Olga said. "Come on, my mother made too much soup, and she's crying too."

qa.a: The paper sign said "Welcome home, idiot."

qa.q: What is Olga feeling when she smiles and cries at once?
qa.a: Joy at seeing Ines, sadness about the three years apart, and probably relief that the wait is over. She says she is not sad, then "a little sad," then "Both."

qa.a: Ines is unsure, because the smile and the tears seem to point different ways, so she pauses instead of guessing. Hearing "Both" settles it.

The college hall was noisy with the alumni reunion, old batchmates slapping backs and comparing grey hairs. Then the lights dimmed for the tribute to Joseph sir, the hostel warden, who had died last year.

His photo came up on the screen: the famous cardigan, the whistle.

Suraj glanced at Pradeep, his old roommate. Pradeep was smiling, wide, the way he used to when Joseph sir caught them sneaking in late. But tears were running down into his collar.

Suraj couldn't tell what he was looking at. Sad? Happy? Both? He didn't want to intrude.

He leaned over and said quietly, "Good tears or hard ones?"

Pradeep laughed and wiped his face. "Both, da. He'd have hated this slideshow."

Suraj put an arm on the back of Pradeep's chair, and they watched the rest of the photos together, sometimes laughing, sometimes silent.

qa.q: Who was being honoured in the tribute?
qa.a: Joseph sir, the hostel warden, who had died last year.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling as he smiled and cried, and how do we know?
qa.a: He felt joy at the memories and sadness at the loss together; he says "Both" and laughs while wiping away tears.

qa.q: How did Suraj support Pradeep, and why did it work?
qa.a: He quietly asked "Good tears or hard ones?" instead of guessing, then simply stayed beside him, which let Pradeep name his mixed feelings.

qa.q: What would change if Suraj had assumed Pradeep was only sad and tried to cheer him up?
qa.a: Pradeep might have felt his happy memories were brushed aside; asking let him show both the joy and the grief.

grounding: It shows a young adult at a reunion reading a friend who smiles and cries at once and simply asking and sharing the moment.

Dear Tushar,

The wedding is over, the relatives have gone, and I finally have a quiet evening, so I'm writing the thing I didn't say on the night.

During the pheras, on the fourth round, I looked at you and you were laughing at something Nisha whispered, and your eyes were full of tears. I froze. For a second I thought something was wrong. Then I wondered if you were thinking of Dadaji, who always said he'd dance at your wedding.

I didn't ask. I just put my hand on your shoulder when you sat down, and you leaned into it.

So I'm asking now: what was it? Happiness, missing him, relief that the planning was over? All of it? I think I'd have felt all of it.

I'm so happy for you both, bhai.

Siddharth

qa.a: Siddharth noticed them on the fourth round.

qa.q: What did Siddharth feel when he saw Tushar laughing with tears in his eyes?
qa.a: Siddharth felt startled and unsure, at first worried something was wrong and then wondering if Tushar was missing Dadaji; Siddharth could not tell which feeling it was.

qa.q: What did Siddharth do in the moment, and why was it enough?
qa.a: Siddharth put a hand on Tushar's shoulder without demanding an explanation, which shared the moment; writing later is a gentle way to ask.

qa.q: How might Tushar feel reading this letter?
qa.a: He will probably feel touched that Siddharth noticed and cared, and may be relieved to say it was many feelings at once.

passage:
Honestly, the best moment of my year was at an airport. I'm Kishore; Dilnaz and I have been friends since school, and I'd gone with her mother to pick her up. She'd been working abroad for three years.

The doors slide open, and there she is with two giant suitcases, and she's grinning so wide, and at the same time she's crying, really crying. Her mother starts crying too, and laughing.

I stood there with the trolley like an idiot. My head was going: is something wrong? Did something happen on the flight? Should I step back and give them space?

So I just asked her, over her mother's shoulder, "Want me to take the bags and give you a minute?"

Dilnaz said, "Stay. I'm fine. It's just everything at once. I'm happy, and I'm sad I missed so much."

Then she pulled me into the hug too.

qa.q: How long had Dilnaz been working abroad?
qa.a: She had been working abroad for three years.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling as she grinned and cried at the airport?
qa.a: She felt happy to be home and sad about everything she had missed, all at once, as she said herself.

qa.q: What helped Kishore handle the moment well?
qa.a: Instead of guessing, Kishore made a simple offer, "Want me to take the bags and give you a minute?", and let Dilnaz say what she needed.

qa.q: What might Dilnaz's mother have been feeling as she cried and laughed too?
qa.a: She was probably overjoyed to have her daughter home after three years, with some sadness for the time apart mixed in.

grounding: It shows a young adult reading a friend who cries and smiles at once at a reunion and simply asking and sharing the moment.

passage: I'm Uma, and I was handing out marigold garlands at my cousin Ganga's wedding when I saw it. The shehnai started for the pheras, and Ganga's face did two things at once. She was smiling so wide her cheeks lifted, and tears were rolling straight down into her dupatta. Her hands trembled on the edge of the mandap. Guests near me whispered. One aunty said, "Nerves." Another said, "Must be missing her father." I didn't know which, or if it was something else. Later, during the photos, I slipped beside her with a tissue. "Happy tears? Or would you like a minute?" She squeezed my hand. "Both. I'm so happy. And Papa would have loved this music." I didn't say anything wise. I just held her hand while the photographer counted to three, and we both smiled through it.
